title: allocation-lifecycle-timeline-and-retention-gaps
content:
Purpose:
Notes from a quick investigation into repeated OOMs on multi-tenant GPUs observed in prod cluster pool-gamma during the 2024-11-12 to 2024-11-14 incident window. This doc focuses on allocation lifecycle timing, short-lived retention gaps (allocations that persist a bit longer than expected), and how those gaps amplify fragmentation and backpressure on cudaMalloc retry paths. Intended audience: serving runtime and infra owners working on allocator heuristics and telemetry.

High-level summary:
- Symptoms: intermittent OOMs on otherwise underutilized GPUs; memory pressure spikes without corresponding persistent resident working set increase; cudaMalloc/async retries that correlate with request latency spikes and subsequent pool-wide degradation.
- Key observation: a small fraction (~3-7%) of requests create allocation waves that survive for an extra 200-800 ms beyond request completion, preventing immediate reuse and causing slab starvation in hot-size classes. Over time these retentions align and cause large contiguous free regions to fragment into many unusable holes.
- Hypothesis: interaction between (a) KV cache churn (evictions that free memory asynchronously), (b) UVM pinned allocations from tokenization/IO paths that rely on host staging buffers, and (c) our slab coalescing code which defers coalescing during high concurrency, causing delayed merging of adjacent free spans. The combination produces both increased small-allocation amplification and failed large contiguous allocation attempts that trigger cudaMalloc async fallback and expensive retries.

Telemetry + evidence:
- Heap timeline capture (sampled every 100ms for 60s) on affected GPU shows repeated patterns: a dozen 64–256 KiB allocations spike per request at t, many freed at t+120ms but ~4–6 allocations remain until t+450ms. These residuals match pattern from tokenization buffer reuse paths.
- Traces show cudaMallocAsync attempts for ~60 MiB contiguous allocation failing with long backoff loops; logs show repeated decommit/coalesce attempts spaced ~250ms apart.
- Per-slab utilization: hot slab sizes (32K, 64K) reach 92% occupancy while mid slabs (2M) drop to 12% free chunk fragmentation — large requests get rejected despite overall free memory being >20%.
- KV cache eviction events correlate with delayed free callbacks: eviction callback runs on a worker thread that schedules page unpin, but the actual device free occurs only after a GC-like walk which is batched; this walk can be delayed under CPU load, extending device retention.

Root-cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Asynchronous free path latency (worker/GC scheduling) causing short retention gaps that prevent immediate chunk reuse. Amplifies when many requests align.
2) Deferment of slab coalescing during high-concurrency to avoid locking causes adjacent free spans to remain separate; later coalescing is batched and may miss windows when large contiguous allocs are needed.
3) UVM/pinned host staging buffers created by tokenization/IO pipeline are freed on host thread but device-side page unpin operates asynchronously and competes with allocator internal lists leading to transient holes.
4) CUDA runtime behavior: repeated cudaMallocAsync-fallbacks throttle the allocator while kernel-level lazy defrag expectations fail (CUDA's allocator may retain pages even after free, depending on driver behavior).

Repro notes & lightweight reproducer idea:
- Pattern to reproduce locally: 1) Start multi-threaded client issuing many small requests (variable token lengths) that allocate 30–200 KiB ephemeral buffers + occasional large contiguous 60–80 MiB requests; 2) make tokenization pipeline allocate pinned host staging buffers that are freed on a different thread; 3) tune GC worker to sleep for 200–500ms to emulate CPU pressure.
- Expectation: after 30–60s the large requests should start failing while small allocation rate remains high; heap profiler should show retention tail at 200–800ms for a set of sizes.

Immediate mitigations tried (quick experiments):
- Lowered GC batching window from 500ms -> 100ms: reduced retention tail amplitude (peak residual count down ~40%), fewer large allocation failures but CPU overhead increased.
- Aggressive per-slab coalescing: immediate coalesce on free reduced fragmentation but increased lock contention; measurable latency regression for some small requests.
- Soft-reserve for large contiguous requests: temporarily reserve a small fraction (~5%) of each GPU for large allocs; avoided many OOMs at cost of slightly reduced apparent capacity.

Longer-term mitigations to evaluate (proposals):
1) Fast-path async-free: implement a low-latency free queue processed on a dedicated allocator thread pinned to a low-latency core to ensure device-side frees occur within ~10–50ms under normal load.
2) Opportunistic coalescing on allocation: when a large allocation fails, trigger immediate coalesce in the requesting thread (best-effort, bounded work) before entering slow retry loop.
3) Adaptive GC window: increase GC batching when system is idle; shrink window when small-allocation rate crosses threshold to avoid retention aggregation.
4) Improve KV-cache eviction path: perform device unpinning synchronously for evictions when free-space is low (fall back to async otherwise). Add a fast-path that marks pages as reclaimable in the allocator without waiting for full decommit.
5) Allocation preflight heuristic: probe for upcoming large requests (from request metadata or rollout config) and proactively compact/prefetch memory.
6) Metrics and alerts: add a "residual-retention" histogram per size-class and an alert when p90 retention > 200ms and large-alloc failure rate > 0.5% over 5m.

Telemetry additions I want to collect next:
- Per-request allocation lifetimes for size classes (histograms with p50/p90/p99 retention).
- Time-to-device-free for each free event (host free -> device free delta).
- Count of failed contiguous large allocation attempts with snapshots of free-span patterns at failure time (lightweight heap fingerprint).
- KV-eviction callback latency distribution and thread scheduling metrics.

Questions / open items:
- Can we change the eviction callback to do synchronous unpin under emergency (low-free) mode without causing CPU stalls upstream? What are the user-facing latency tradeoffs?
- Are there driver-level knobs (CUDA or driver config) to reduce device-side retention after free on our target instance types?
- Would a per-tenant soft-reserve for large allocations be acceptable as a temporary protective measure while we iterate on allocator changes?

Action items:
- (Priya) Build the local reproducer and collect heap-snapshot timelines (due 2024-11-22).
- (Marco) Prototype fast-path async-free worker thread and measure delta in retention (due 2024-11-29).
- (Jill) Add the retention histogram metric and alert in telemetry backlog (create ticket: JIRA-RT-3421).
- (Kenji) Evaluate per-slab on-free coalesce cost and produce microbench (due 2024-12-06).

Appendix: quick sketch of heap-fingerprint (lightweight) to capture on large-allocation failure:
- sample free-list head pointers for top N slabs + counts, record largest free-span length and number of spans > 1MiB, attach small stack trace of requesting thread. Keep sample size tiny (<2KB) to avoid noise.

Notes to self: when writing up for eng-sync, include a short diagram of allocation waves vs GC window showing how alignment produces contiguous hole fragmentation. Also call out interaction with padding strategy (we currently pad per-batch to 64-token boundary which increases small alloc counts; re-evaluate benefits vs fragmentation cost).

End of notes.
